title: Living water (John 4:7–15)
hook: whoever drinks the water I give shall not thirst for ever

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bridegroom's friend: he must increase, but I must decrease. Your line was he must increase. Who got the credit from you? Day five hundred. Five hundred days on the path.

Noon in Samaria. The sixth hour, John says, the hottest part of the day. Nobody goes to the well at noon. You draw water in the cool of the morning, with the other women, talking. But one woman comes alone, at noon, with her jar. Sitting on the edge of Jacob's well, tired from the road, is a Jewish man. Jews and Samaritans had a long and bitter history; they didn't share cups. Men didn't strike up conversations with women they didn't know. And then he speaks to her, and his first words are a request.
screen: `NOON AT JACOB'S WELL.` → `A WOMAN COMES ALONE.` → `A TIRED STRANGER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: He says: "Give me to drink." God, in John's Gospel, begins by asking. She's startled. How do you, a Jew, ask a drink of me, a Samaritan woman? And he answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "If thou didst know the gift of God, and who he is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou perhaps wouldst have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water." Living water. In everyday speech then, living water meant running water: a spring, a stream, water that moves, as opposed to the still water collected in a cistern. So she takes him literally and very practically. Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well? He doesn't argue about Jacob. He points at the bucket. Whoever drinks this water will be thirsty again. Tomorrow at noon she'll be back with the jar. "But he that shall drink of the water that I will give him, shall not thirst for ever." It becomes a spring inside, welling up into everlasting life. And she says the most human thing: Sir, give me this water, so I don't have to keep coming here. She still thinks it's about the walk to the well. The Catechism opens its teaching on prayer with this scene. It says that Jesus thirsts, and his asking comes from the depth of God's desire for us. Prayer, it says, whether we know it or not, is the meeting of God's thirst with ours. The one who began by asking for a drink is the one who has the water.
screen: `GIVE ME TO DRINK.` · `LIVING WATER: RUNNING WATER.` · `THIS WATER, THIRSTY AGAIN.` · `GOD'S THIRST MEETS OURS.` · then, large: `SHALL NOT THIRST FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink water slowly and pray. Get a glass of water if you can. Settle, and breathe. Lift the glass and feel its weight. Take one slow sip, and notice the cool of it going down. Then another. Think of the thirst underneath this one: the thing you keep going back to the well for, that never quite fills you. If you pray, you can ask, as she did, give me this water. If you don't, just drink slowly and pay attention to being thirsty and being given something. The bell holds the time.
Living water. Running, spring water in everyday speech; in John, the gift Jesus offers at Jacob's well that ends thirst for ever. Today's word.
Your line: never thirst. Today, every time you drink water, let it remind you of the one who asked first. Day five hundred.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the woman at the well on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year A, often with adults preparing for baptism at Easter, and the Catechism begins its teaching on prayer with this scene.

options: move to the other side of the well.

original.note: Greek: living water (John 4:10), the ordinary phrase for running, spring water.

trapdoor: what you thought: living water is a poetic phrase Jesus made up.
what it means: everyday speech for running water, which Jesus fills with a new meaning: a spring of everlasting life.
what a scholar hears: hydōr zōn is the term for flowing water; the Catechism (2560) reads the scene as God's thirst meeting ours in prayer.
